claim: Medaka (Oryzias latipes) and zebrafish (Danio rerio) shared their last common ancestor between 200 and 300 million years ago.
source: To investigate MG cell-mediated retina regeneration in a distantly related teleost, we chose the Japanese ricefish medaka (Oryzias latipes), which is a well-established model organism that shared its last common ancestor with zebrafish between 200 and 300 million years ago (Schartl et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schartl et al., 2013

claim: Medaka fins can be fully regenerated in adults.
source: Whereas fins can be fully regenerated in adult medaka (Nakatani et al., 2007), the heart has no regenerative capacity (Ito et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakatani et al., 2007

claim: Medaka heart has no regenerative capacity.
source: Whereas fins can be fully regenerated in adult medaka (Nakatani et al., 2007), the heart has no regenerative capacity (Ito et al., 2014; Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2014 and Lai et al., 2017

claim: Sox2 is well known for its role in maintaining the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells.
source: Sox2 is well known for its role in maintaining the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (Masui et al., 2007) and is one of the four original Yamanaka factors required for the generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Masui et al., 2007

claim: Sox2 is one of the four original Yamanaka factors required for the generation of induced pluripotent stem cells.
source: Sox2 is well known for its role in maintaining the pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (Masui et al., 2007) and is one of the four original Yamanaka factors required for the generation of induced pluripotent stem cells (Takahashi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takahashi et al., 2007

claim: Sox2 has been used to convert mouse and human fibroblasts directly into induced neural stem cells.
source: Sox2 has been frequently used in reprogramming studies, such as the conversion of mouse and human fibroblasts directly into induced neural stem cells (Ring et al., 2012), or the transformation of NG2 glia into functional neurons following stab lesions in the adult mouse cerebral cortex (Heinrich et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ring et al., 2012

claim: Sox2 has been used to transform NG2 glia into functional neurons following stab lesions in the adult mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Sox2 has been frequently used in reprogramming studies, such as the conversion of mouse and human fibroblasts directly into induced neural stem cells (Ring et al., 2012), or the transformation of NG2 glia into functional neurons following stab lesions in the adult mouse cerebral cortex (Heinrich et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heinrich et al., 2014

claim: In the regenerating zebrafish retina, sox2 expression is upregulated 2 days post injury.
source: In the regenerating zebrafish retina, sox2 expression is upregulated 2 days post injury (dpi) and is necessary and sufficient for the MG proliferation associated with regeneration (Ramachandran et al., 2010; Gorsuch et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ramachandran et al., 2010 and Gorsuch et al., 2017

claim: Sox2 is necessary and sufficient for MG proliferation associated with regeneration in zebrafish retina.
source: In the regenerating zebrafish retina, sox2 expression is upregulated 2 days post injury (dpi) and is necessary and sufficient for the MG proliferation associated with regeneration (Ramachandran et al., 2010; Gorsuch et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ramachandran et al., 2010 and Gorsuch et al., 2017

claim: Medaka Müller glia cells behave like progenitors and exhibit a restricted capacity to regenerate the retina.
source: In contrast to zebrafish, medaka Müller glia (olMG) cells behave like progenitors and exhibit a restricted capacity to regenerate the retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing limited regenerative capacity of olMG cells

claim: After injury, olMG cells proliferate but fail to self-renew.
source: After injury, olMG cells proliferate but fail to self-renew and ultimately only restore photoreceptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including BrdU lineage tracing and immunohistochemistry

claim: After injury, olMG cells ultimately only restore photoreceptors.
source: After injury, olMG cells proliferate but fail to self-renew and ultimately only restore photoreceptors.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5

claim: In contrast to zebrafish, proliferating olMG cells do not maintain sox2 expression after injury.
source: In our injury paradigm, we observed that in contrast to zebrafish, proliferating olMG cells do not maintain sox2 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6

claim: Sustained sox2 expression in olMG cells confers regenerative responses similar to those of zebrafish MG cells.
source: Sustained sox2 expression in olMG cells confers regenerative responses similar to those of zebrafish MG (drMG) cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sox2 overexpression experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8

claim: A single, cell-autonomous factor reprograms olMG cells and establishes a regeneration-like mode.
source: We show that a single, cell-autonomous factor reprograms olMG cells and establishes a regeneration-like mode.
evidence: The claim is supported by sox2 overexpression experiments demonstrating cell-autonomous reprogramming

claim: The retina of teleost fishes undergoes lifelong neurogenesis.
source: The retina of these fish undergoes lifelong neurogenesis, and the range of retinal cell types is generated from two sources.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about teleost fish retinal development

claim: The ciliary marginal zone (CMZ) includes retinal stem cells that give rise to progenitor cells and ultimately differentiated cell types of the growing neural retina.
source: The first are the cells of the ciliary marginal zone (CMZ), which include retinal stem cells that give rise to progenitor cells and ultimately differentiated cell types of the growing neural retina (Centanin et al., 2011, 2014; Raymond et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Centanin et al., 2011, 2014 and Raymond et al., 2006

claim: Müller glia cells generate new cell types during homeostasis and regeneration in teleost fish.
source: A second source for new retinal cells are Müller glia (MG) cells, which generate new cell types during homeostasis and regeneration (Bernardos et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bernardos et al., 2007

claim: Zebrafish contains multipotent MG cells which can self-renew and regenerate all retinal neuronal and glial cell types after injuries.
source: Among these, zebrafish is the best-studied and has been shown to contain multipotent MG cells which can self-renew and regenerate all retinal neuronal and glial cell types after injuries.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about zebrafish retinal regeneration

claim: olMG cells are quiescent at a comparable developmental stage in the hatchling (8 dpf) retina.
source: In contrast to zebrafish and goldfish, where MG cells are described as the source of rod PRCs that gradually accumulate during the early larval period (Bernardos et al., 2007; Nelson et al., 2008), it has been shown previously that olMG cells are quiescent at a comparable developmental stage in the hatchling (8 dpf) retina (Lust et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lust et al., 2016

claim: The zebrafish retina massively increases its rod PRC number during post-embryonic growth via the proliferation of MG cells.
source: While the zebrafish retina massively increases its rod PRC number during post-embryonic growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B''') via the proliferation of MG cells (Bernardos et al., 2007), the medaka retina maintains its rod PRC layer from embryonic to adult stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D''') and rod PRCs are born from the CMZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bernardos et al., 2007 and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B'''

claim: The medaka retina maintains its rod PRC layer from embryonic to adult stages.
source: While the zebrafish retina massively increases its rod PRC number during post-embryonic growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B''') via the proliferation of MG cells (Bernardos et al., 2007), the medaka retina maintains its rod PRC layer from embryonic to adult stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D''') and rod PRCs are born from the CMZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D'''

claim: In medaka, rod PRCs are born from the CMZ.
source: While the zebrafish retina massively increases its rod PRC number during post-embryonic growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B''') via the proliferation of MG cells (Bernardos et al., 2007), the medaka retina maintains its rod PRC layer from embryonic to adult stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D''') and rod PRCs are born from the CMZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The rx2::H2B-eGFP transgenic line labels the CMZ, olMG cells and cone PRCs but no rods in hatchling (8dpf) and adult medaka.
source: In order to address the regenerative abilities of olMG cells we used the rx2::H2B-eGFP transgenic line that labels the CMZ, olMG cells and cone PRCs but no rods in hatchling (8dpf) and adult medaka (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Reinhardt et al., 2015) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009 and Reinhardt et al., 2015, and by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Proliferating cells are detected in the central retina 3 days after needle injury in medaka.
source: We detected proliferating cells in the central retina, on the basis of both labels PH3 (Figure 1A–1A'') and BrdU (Figure 1B–1B'') 3 days after a needle injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A–1A'' and Figure 1B–1B''

claim: Proliferating cells after injury co-localize with rx2-driven H2B-eGFP, showing that olMG cells had re-entered the cell cycle.
source: These proliferating cells were also positive for rx2-driven H2B-eGFP, showing that the olMG cells had re-entered the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization in Figure 1

claim: olMG cells in hatchling medaka are quiescent in an uninjured background.
source: These results demonstrate that olMG cells in hatchling medaka are quiescent in an uninjured background (Lust et al., 2016), but begin to proliferate upon injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lust et al., 2016

claim: olMG cells begin to proliferate upon injury.
source: These results demonstrate that olMG cells in hatchling medaka are quiescent in an uninjured background (Lust et al., 2016), but begin to proliferate upon injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing BrdU and PH3 positive cells after injury

claim: The onset of MG proliferation in zebrafish has been observed between 1 and 2 dpi.
source: The onset of MG proliferation in zebrafish has been observed between 1 and 2 dpi (Fausett and Goldman, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fausett and Goldman, 2006

claim: At 1 dpi, no BrdU-positive cells were detected in the medaka retina after injury.
source: At 1 dpi, no BrdU-positive cells were detected in the retina (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations

claim: At 2 dpi, the first BrdU-positive cells were detected in the INL and ONL of the central retina in medaka.
source: At 2 dpi, the first BrdU-positive cells were detected in the inner nuclear layer (INL) and the outer nuclear layer (ONL) of the central retina (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B''').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B'''

claim: olMG cells start re-entering the cell cycle between 1 and 2 dpi.
source: These results show that olMG cells start re-entering the cell cycle between 1 and 2 dpi but do not generate neurogenic clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU incorporation data at different time points

claim: olMG cells do not generate neurogenic clusters after injury.
source: These results show that olMG cells start re-entering the cell cycle between 1 and 2 dpi but do not generate neurogenic clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with zebrafish showing single or paired BrdU-positive cells rather than clusters

claim: In response to injury olMG cells initiate DNA synthesis and divide maximally once as indicated by the appearance of single or a maximum of two BrdU-positive cells next to each other in the INL at both 2 dpi and 3 dpi.
source: In response to injury olMG cells initiate DNA synthesis and divide maximally once as indicated by the appearance of single or a maximum of two BrdU-positive cells next to each other in the INL at both 2 dpi and 3 dpi (Figure 1C and C').
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 1C and C'

claim: The injury response of zebrafish MG cells at comparable stages (4dpf) is characterized by the formation of large nuclear, neurogenic clusters in the INL.
source: In contrast, the injury response of zebrafish MG (drMG) cells at comparable stages (4dpf) is characterized by the formation of large nuclear, neurogenic clusters in the INL (Figure 1D and D').
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and D'

claim: In adult zebrafish, a single asymmetric division of drMG cells produces a MG cell and a progenitor cell that divides rapidly to generate neurogenic clusters.
source: This is consistent with the response of adult drMG cells to injury in which a single asymmetric division produces a MG cell and a progenitor cell that divides rapidly to generate neurogenic clusters (Nagashima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nagashima et al., 2013

claim: olMG nuclei below the wound site started migrating apically at 17 hpi after PRC injuries.
source: We induced PRC injuries in medaka and observed that olMG nuclei below the wound site started migrating apically at 17 hpi (Figure 2A–2A''', see also Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2A–2A'''

claim: Nuclear migrations after PRC injury were not coordinated between individual cells.
source: These migrations were not coordinated between individual cells.
evidence: The claim is based on observations from in vivo imaging

claim: After RGC injuries, there was no migration of olMG nuclei within the first 30 hpi.
source: In contrast, after RGC injuries, there was no migration of olMG nuclei, either apically or basally toward the wound, within the first 30 hpi (Figure 2B–2B''', see also Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2B–2B'''

claim: At 2 dpi, retinae with PRC injuries showed a gap in the INL below the injury site, at a position where olMG nuclei are normally found.
source: At 2 dpi, retinae with PRC injuries showed a gap in the INL below the injury site, at a position where olMG nuclei are normally found, reflecting the migration of olMG nuclei towards the ONL from this location (Figure 2C–2C'').
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2C–2C''

claim: The gap in the INL after PRC injury persisted until 6 dpi.
source: The gap in the INL persisted until 6 dpi (Figure 2C'').
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2C''

claim: No migration of olMG nuclei was observed after RGC injuries until 6 dpi.
source: Here, we neither observed an apical nor basal migration of olMG nuclei (Figure 2D–2D'') and in fact no migration of olMG nuclei was observed at all until 6 dpi.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2D–2D''

claim: Large RGC injuries led to swelling and secondary cell death of PRCs and activated olMG nuclei to migrate apically.
source: To rule out that this is due to too little damage in the RGC layer we increased the injury size. This led to swelling and secondary cell death of PRCs and activated olMG nuclei to migrate apically (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B), indicating further that their preferential reaction is toward PRC injuries.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B

claim: olMG nuclei migrate toward PRC injury sites within 24 hpi and remain in this location up until 6 days.
source: Taken together, these results show that olMG nuclei migrate toward PRC injury sites within 24 hpi and remain in this location up until 6 days, whereas they display no discernible reaction toward RGC injuries.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data from Figure 2

claim: olMG cells display no discernible reaction toward RGC injuries.
source: Taken together, these results show that olMG nuclei migrate toward PRC injury sites within 24 hpi and remain in this location up until 6 days, whereas they display no discernible reaction toward RGC injuries.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data from Figure 2

claim: olMG nuclei migrated out of the INL into the wound site after ONL injuries.
source: As previously observed, olMG nuclei migrated out of the INL into the wound site (Figure 3A–3A'').
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A–3A''

claim: The rx2::lifeact-eGFP labeled cell bodies of the olMG cells spanning the entire apico-basal distance remained intact until 6 dpi in the absence of an apparent nucleus in the INL.
source: The rx2::lifeact-eGFP labeled cell bodies of the olMG cells spanning the entire apico-basal distance remained intact until 6 dpi in the absence of an apparent (labeled) nucleus in the INL (Figure 3A'').
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 3A''

claim: At the site of injury, GFP-positive cell bodies did not contain a nucleus anymore while neighboring, more distant GFP-positive cell bodies contained elongated olMG nuclei at 3 dpi.
source: After injury, incubation in BrdU for 3 days and direct fixation at 3 dpi we found that at the site of injury the GFP-positive cell bodies, labeled by rx2::lifeact-eGFP, did not contain a nucleus anymore while the neighboring, more distant GFP-positive cell bodies contained elongated olMG nuclei (Figure 3B–B'''', see also Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B–B''''

claim: At 10 dpi, the majority of olMG nuclei were absent from the INL in the region directly underneath the site of injury.
source: After incubation in BrdU for 3 days and fixation at 10 dpi, we observed similar results (Figure 3C–3C''). Here, we used immunohistochemistry to detect the olMG cell bodies via a GS-staining (Figure 3C). BrdU-positive cells in the ONL mark the site of the injury (Figure 3C''). In the region directly underneath the site of injury, the majority of olMG nuclei, which had been labeled by rx2::H2B-eGFP, were absent from the INL (Figure 3C'').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C–3C''

claim: GS-positive cell bodies remained spanning the entire apico-basal height without the apparent presence of nuclei after injury.
source: GS-positive cell bodies remained spanning the entire apico-basal height, but without the apparent presence of nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from Figure 3

claim: The cell bodies of injury-activated olMG cells are still intact despite the migration of their nuclei into the ONL.
source: This data shows that the cell bodies of injury-activated olMG cells are still intact despite the migration of their nuclei into the ONL.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in vivo imaging data from Figure 3

claim: PH3-positive cells were detected only in the INL after injury in medaka.
source: We detected PH3-positive cells only in the INL (Figure 4A–4A'').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A–4A''

claim: In zebrafish, PH3-positive drMG cells can be found in the ONL 2 days after injury in a light injury paradigm.
source: This is in contrast to findings in zebrafish where, in a light injury paradigm, PH3-positive drMG cells can be found in the ONL 2 days after injury (Nagashima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nagashima et al., 2013

claim: The first injury-triggered olMG divisions were observed at 44 hpi.
source: The first injury-triggered olMG divisions were observed at 44 hpi (Figure 4B–4B''', see also Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data shown in Figure 4B–4B'''

claim: The mode of division of olMG cells was preferentially apico-basal (5 out of 6 divisions in 5 out of 6 animals).
source: The mode of division was preferentially apico-basal (5 out of 6 divisions in 5 out of 6 animals), while only a single horizontal division was observed (1 out of 6 divisions in 1 out of 6 animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data quantifying division orientation

claim: drMG cells are reported to predominantly divide with a horizontal division plane.
source: In contrast, drMG cells are reported to predominantly divide with a horizontal division plane (Lahne et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lahne et al., 2015

claim: Injury-induced olMG cell divisions occur in different positions in the INL and have a strong preference to occur apico-basally.
source: These results show that injury-induced olMG cell divisions occur in different positions in the INL and have a strong preference to occur apico-basally.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo imaging data from Figure 4

claim: In zebrafish, drMG cells are able to regenerate all neuronal cell types and self-renew after injury.
source: In zebrafish, drMG cells are able to regenerate all neuronal cell types and self-renew after injury (Nagashima et al., 2013; Powell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nagashima et al., 2013 and Powell et al., 2016

claim: PRC injuries led to the detection of 97% of all BrdU-positive cells in the ONL, mostly in the rod nuclear layer.
source: PRC injuries led to the detection of 97% of all BrdU-positive cells in the ONL, mostly in the rod nuclear layer, indicative for PRC fate (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5B and E

claim: No BrdU-positive cells could be detected in the INL after PRC injuries.
source: No BrdU-positive cells could be detected in the INL.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data from Figure 5

claim: The INL below the injury site was devoid of olMG cell nuclei after PRC injuries.
source: Additionally, we found that the INL below the injury site was devoid of olMG cell nuclei, both consistently arguing for the absence of injury-triggered olMG self-renewal.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data from Figure 5

claim: RGC injuries did not trigger BrdU-uptake in olMG cells or any other differentiated cell type.
source: Strikingly, RGC injuries did not trigger BrdU-uptake in olMG cells or any other differentiated cell type (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations

claim: Needle injuries affecting all retinal cell types triggered the same response as the specific lesions in the PRC layer, with 97% of all BrdU-positive cells present in the ONL.
source: Needle injuries affecting all retinal cell types triggered the same response as the specific lesions in the PRC layer. 97% of all BrdU-positive cells were present in the ONL, and only a single BrdU-positive olMG cell was found in 1 of 10 fish (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5C and E

claim: Later application of BrdU after injury (4 to 7 dpi) did not result in BrdU-positive olMG cells.
source: Also later application of BrdU after injury (4 to 7 dpi) did not result in BrdU-positive olMG cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: BrdU-positive nuclei were not positive for GS, indicating that they were not olMG cells anymore.
source: Importantly, BrdU-positive nuclei were not positive for GS, indicating that they were not olMG cells anymore (Figure 5D), but were positive for Recoverin, a PRC marker (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: BrdU-positive nuclei were positive for Recoverin, a PRC marker.
source: Importantly, BrdU-positive nuclei were not positive for GS, indicating that they were not olMG cells anymore (Figure 5D), but were positive for Recoverin, a PRC marker (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E

claim: olMG cells do not self-renew and rather function as mono-potent repair system restricted to the generation of PRCs, most of which belong to the rod lineage.
source: These results demonstrate that olMG cells do not self-renew and rather function as mono-potent repair system restricted to the generation of PRCs, most of which belong to the rod lineage.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data from Figure 5

claim: In the medaka retina, Sox2 protein is detected in amacrine cells (ACs) and olMG cells in the central retina.
source: In the medaka retina, Sox2 protein is detected in amacrine cells (ACs) and olMG cells in the central retina (Figure 6A–6A''').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A–6A'''

claim: In zebrafish, Sox2 protein is present in ACs and drMG cells in the central retina.
source: In zebrafish, the pattern is similar: Sox2 protein is present in ACs and drMG cells in the central retina (Figure 6B–6B''').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B–6B'''

claim: MG cells in many other vertebrates, including humans, maintain sox2 expression.
source: This data is consistent with data from other vertebrates including human, whose MG cells also maintain sox2 expression (Gallina et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gallina et al., 2014

claim: Sox2 expression in olMG cells is downregulated in response to injury.
source: However, sox2 expression in olMG cells is downregulated in response to injury, in contrast to the injury response of drMG cells, which upregulate sox2 (Gorsuch et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from Figure 6 and citation to Gorsuch et al., 2017

claim: drMG cells upregulate sox2 in response to injury.
source: However, sox2 expression in olMG cells is downregulated in response to injury, in contrast to the injury response of drMG cells, which upregulate sox2 (Gorsuch et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gorsuch et al., 2017

claim: The vast majority of proliferating olMG cells did not express sox2 anymore at 3 dpi (6% of all BrdU-positive cells were Sox2-positive).
source: The vast majority of proliferating olMG cells did not express sox2 anymore at 3 dpi (Figure 6C–6D, 6% of all BrdU-positive cells were Sox2-positive).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6C–6D

claim: In zebrafish, sox2 expression was still detected after 3 days in drMG cells that proliferated in response to needle injury (84% of all BrdU-positive cells were Sox2-positive).
source: Conversely, in zebrafish, sox2 expression was still detected after 3 days in drMG cells that proliferated in response to needle injury (Figure 6E–6F, 84% of all BrdU-positive cells were Sox2-positive).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E–6F

claim: The downregulation of sox2 expression in proliferating olMG cells restricts their regenerative properties.
source: These findings strongly argue that the downregulation of sox2 expression in proliferating olMG cells restricts their regenerative properties.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the sox2 expression data and comparison with zebrafish

claim: Increased levels of Sox2 protein were detected in mifepristone-treated olMG cells in rx2::LexPR OP::sox2, OP::H2B-eGFP transgenic fish.
source: In mifepristone-treated retinae, we detected increased levels of Sox2 protein in induced olMG cells (Figure 7A–B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7A–B''

claim: Increased formation of proliferating clusters and distribution of BrdU-positive cells in all layers of the retina were observed after needle injury in sox2-induced fish (4 out of 6 fish).
source: We observed increased formation of proliferating clusters as well as the distribution of BrdU-positive cells in all layers of the retina after needle injury (4 out of 6 fish) (Figure 7D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7D–E'

claim: In needle-injured wild-type fish treated with mifepristone, olMG cells did not self-renew and gave predominantly rise to PRCs, mostly rod PRCs.
source: In needle-injured wild-type fish which were also treated with mifepristone as well as in transgenic fish (rx2::LexPR OP::sox2, OP::H2B-eGFP) which were not treated with mifepristone, olMG cells did not self-renew and gave predominantly rise to PRCs, mostly rod PRCs (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 8F

claim: olMG cells maintaining sox2 expression after injury showed self-renewal and differentiation into different cell types in the ONL and INL.
source: In contrast, olMG cells experiencing persistent expression of sox2 showed self-renewal and differentiation into different cell types in the ONL and INL as indicated by BrdU lineage tracing.
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data from Figure 8

claim: olMG cells maintaining sox2 expression after injury regenerated olMG cells.
source: In particular, the olMG cells maintaining sox2 expression after injury regenerated olMG cells (Figure 8C–C'' and F) and exhibited a significant increase in regenerated ACs and RGCs, which were positive for HuC/D (Figure 7D–E'' and 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 8C–C'' and F

claim: olMG cells maintaining sox2 expression after injury exhibited a significant increase in regenerated ACs and RGCs.
source: In particular, the olMG cells maintaining sox2 expression after injury regenerated olMG cells (Figure 8C–C'' and F) and exhibited a significant increase in regenerated ACs and RGCs, which were positive for HuC/D (Figure 7D–E'' and 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7D–E'' and 8F

claim: A slight increase in cone PRCs and a decrease in rod PRCs was observed after sox2 induction.
source: Furthermore, a slight increase in cone PRCs and a decrease in rod PRCs was observed after sox2 induction (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 8C–F

claim: A targeted maintenance of sox2 expression after injury is sufficient to induce self-renewal and increase potency in olMG cells in the medaka retina.
source: These data indicate that a targeted maintenance of sox2 expression after injury is sufficient to induce self-renewal and increase potency in olMG cells in the medaka retina turning a mono-potent repair system into a regeneration system with increased potency.
evidence: The claim is supported by sox2 overexpression experiments from Figures 7 and 8

claim: olMG cells do not self-renew after injuries and only have the capacity to regenerate PRCs, therefore they are not true multipotent retinal stem cells.
source: Since olMG cells do not self-renew after injuries and only have the capacity to regenerate PRCs, olMG cells are not true multipotent retinal stem cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing limited regenerative capacity

claim: olMG cells should be considered lineage-restricted progenitors.
source: Instead, olMG cells should be considered lineage-restricted progenitors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing limited regenerative capacity

claim: olMG cells re-enter the cell cycle between 1 and 2 dpi, similar to the re-entry observed in zebrafish.
source: They re-enter the cell cycle between 1 and 2 dpi, similar to the re-entry observed in zebrafish.
evidence: The claim is supported by BrdU incorporation data from Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The signals that are essential for cell cycle re-entry are present in medaka and are activated in a window of time similar to that in zebrafish.
